channel.title: Training on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Training on Best of AI

item.title: Anki
item.description:
Users create cards or download shared decks, and the app shows each card just before they would forget it. Add-ons add features, and sync works across devices. The desktop app is free.

The iOS app is paid, and the interface is plain.

Quizlet and RemNote are alternatives. Anki suits students who need long-term retention.

item.title: Brisk Teaching
item.description:
Teachers can generate lesson materials, adjust reading levels, and draft feedback on student writing. A student-facing feature lets pupils chat with an AI tutor under teacher guidance. It also supports quizzes.

A free plan covers basic features, and paid plans add more. Teachers should check output before using it with students.

MagicSchool and Diffit are alternatives. Brisk Teaching suits educators who work in Google Workspace.

item.title: Diffit
item.description:
Teachers paste in a source and choose a grade level. Diffit produces a summary, vocabulary list, and questions. Resources can be exported to Google Docs and Slides.

The free plan has limits, and paid plans remove them.

MagicSchool and Brisk Teaching offer broader teacher tools. Diffit suits educators who differentiate reading materials.

item.title: GeoGebra
item.description:
Users draw geometric objects, define functions, and drag points to see relationships change. It includes graphing, spreadsheet, and 3D tools. A large library of shared activities covers school topics.

It runs in a browser and on phones and tablets.

Desmos is a close alternative for graphing. GeoGebra suits mathematicians and teachers who explore ideas visually.

item.title: Goalbook
item.description:
Teachers pick learning targets, choose research-based strategies, and build goals aligned to standards. Teams use shared planning tools to track progress. Some AI features help draft IEP language.

Schools and districts license it. Teachers should check AI-drafted language against the student’s data.

Frontline and SpEd Forms are IEP software alternatives. Goalbook suits special education teachers.

item.title: Google Classroom
item.description:
Teachers create classes, share materials from Drive, and grade submissions. Students see due dates and turn in work. Gemini features help teachers draft lesson plans and quiz questions in education plans.

It is free for Google Workspace for Education accounts and works well with Docs and Meet.

Canvas and Schoology are fuller learning management systems. Google Classroom suits educators who already use Google tools.

item.title: Gradescope
item.description:
Students submit scans or online work. Graders mark answers by clicking rubric items, and changing a rubric item updates every submission that used it. AI-assisted grouping clusters similar answers so one grading decision can apply to many students. Code assignments can be autograded.

It is common in university STEM courses with large enrollments. Regrade requests and grading analytics are built in, and it connects to most learning management systems.

Institutions pay for access. Canvas SpeedGrader and Crowdmark are alternatives. Gradescope suits instructors and teaching assistants who grade many similar assignments.

item.title: Kahoot!
item.description:
A host runs a quiz, and players join with a code and answer on phones or laptops. Scores appear after each question. AI features can generate questions from a topic or a document.

A free version covers basic games, and paid plans add reports and larger groups.

Quizizz and Mentimeter are alternatives. Kahoot! suits educators who want energetic review sessions.

item.title: MoeGo
item.description:
Groomers see appointments by staff and van, store pet profiles, and send reminders. Customers book online and pay by card. AI answers calls and messages in some plans.

It is a subscription product.

Gingr and Pawfinity are alternatives. MoeGo suits pet groomers and small pet service shops.

item.title: Touch Surgery
item.description:
Surgeons and trainees practice steps of a procedure on a phone or tablet. Teams record surgeries and use AI to find phases and generate reports. Hospitals use it for education and quality review.

Content and access vary between free and enterprise tiers.

Osmo and Proximie are related platforms. Touch Surgery suits surgeons and surgical assistants.

item.title: TrainingPeaks
item.description:
It imports data from watches and bike computers and calculates load, fitness, and fatigue. Coaches assign workouts and see compliance. Premium plans add advanced analysis.

It is data heavy, and its value depends on regular logging.

Strava and Intervals.icu are alternatives. TrainingPeaks suits coaches and athletes who follow structured plans.

item.title: TrueCoach
item.description:
Coaches assign workouts from an exercise library, and clients log sets in an app. Messaging and progress photos keep communication in one place. Plans are priced by client count.

It focuses on programming and communication, and billing tools are lighter than in all-in-one platforms.

Trainerize and Everfit are alternatives. TrueCoach suits fitness coaches.

item.title: 360Learning
item.description:
360Learning is based on the idea that the people who know a topic best are usually inside the company, not in a training department. Experts build short courses with the platform’s authoring tool, colleagues give feedback in comments, and learners can ask questions that feed back into the material. It is called collaborative learning.

The platform covers the usual LMS functions: assigning training, tracking completion, compliance, and reporting. Learning paths and skills features help manage development, and integrations connect with HR and communication tools. An AI assistant generates outlines, lessons, and quiz questions from documents, which reduces the time needed to create content.

item.title: Adobe Captivate
item.description:
Captivate is a long-standing tool for instructional designers. They build courses from slides with interactive elements like quizzes, branching scenarios, drag and drop exercises, and video. A standout feature is software simulation, where the tool records on-screen steps in an application and turns them into demonstrations or practice exercises, which helps train employees on new systems.

Courses are responsive, so they work on desktops and mobile devices, and they publish in formats that learning management systems can track, including SCORM, xAPI, and HTML5. Assets from Adobe’s other tools can be reused. Recent versions add AI help, such as text to speech for narration and automatic generation of some content.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker
item.description: SageMaker started as a way to run machine learning on AWS without managing servers. Data scientists use notebooks to prepare data and write code, then train models on managed compute that scales up as needed. Once a model is trained, SageMaker can deploy it behind an endpoint, monitor its performance, and handle versioning, which turns a notebook experiment into a production service. It supports popular frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow.

item.title: Autodesk Fusion
item.description: Fusion combines the steps of making a physical product in one application. You model parts and assemblies in 3D, run simulations to test stress and heat, and generate toolpaths for CNC machines and 3D printers. It also includes electronics design and drawing tools. Because it runs with cloud-connected data, teams can share designs and collaborate, and it works on both Windows and macOS. Product designers, engineers, machinists, and hobbyists all use it.

item.title: BigQuery
item.description: BigQuery lets teams analyze huge amounts of data without managing servers. You load data from files, databases, streams, or other Google services, write SQL, and BigQuery spreads the work across many machines and returns results quickly, whether the table holds millions or trillions of rows. Because storage and compute are separated and managed, there is no cluster to size or tune, which is a big reason analytics teams like it.

item.title: Brainly
item.description:
Brainly grew from a Q&A site for students. A learner posts a question, other users and moderators answer it, and the best responses are verified. Over time, it has built a large library of questions and answers across math, science, languages, and history, with versions for many countries that follow local curricula.

The product now blends community with AI. An AI tutor gives step-by-step explanations, can solve problems from a photo, and helps with writing and study guides. A paid plan removes ads and unlocks more AI help and expert-verified answers. Some features are free with limits.

item.title: Bria
item.description:
Bria builds visual generative AI around licensing. Its models are trained on licensed data from content partners rather than scraped web images, and contributors share in revenue, which gives companies a clearer position on copyright than many alternatives. The company also offers indemnification to enterprise customers.

The product is delivered as APIs and tools for businesses. Capabilities include generating images from prompts, editing and background removal, creating product shots, and controls for brand consistency. Enterprises in advertising, e-commerce, and media can embed these features in their apps, with options for fine-tuning on their own assets.

item.title: Cornerstone OnDemand
item.description:
Cornerstone OnDemand is one of the established vendors of learning management systems. Large employers use it to host training, assign compliance courses, track completion, and manage development plans. The platform covers learning, performance reviews, succession planning, and a content library from outside providers.

Its newer direction centers on skills. AI infers the skills employees have from their roles and activity, compares them to what jobs require, and recommends courses and career paths. Generative AI helps create content, summarize learning, and give managers guidance. The aim is to move from course catalogs to skill growth.

item.title: Course Hero
item.description:
Course Hero started as a library of materials uploaded by students from their classes. Learners search for notes, practice problems, and study guides tied to specific courses and schools, and unlock documents by uploading their own or paying for a subscription. Tutors answer questions on a range of subjects.

An AI assistant now sits alongside the library. It explains concepts, helps with study guides and flashcards, and answers questions about uploaded materials. This makes the site more of a general study tool than a document repository, though the document library remains the main draw for many users.

item.title: DataCamp
item.description:
DataCamp is built around learning by doing. Each lesson combines a few minutes of video with exercises you complete in an in-browser editor, so you write real code with immediate feedback and no setup. Courses cover Python, R, SQL, Excel, Power BI, statistics, machine learning, and more recently AI and large language models, taught by instructors from industry and academia.

Structured paths help learners progress. Career tracks, such as data analyst or data scientist, string together courses and projects, skill assessments show strengths and gaps, and certifications validate skills for employers. An AI assistant gives hints and explains errors, and a workspace allows practice in notebooks. Teams can buy it for corporate training with reporting.

item.title: Google Cloud Vision
item.description:
Google Cloud Vision is a set of pretrained image analysis features available through an API. Send an image, and it can return labels describing what it contains, detect objects and their locations, read printed and handwritten text, identify landmarks and logos, detect faces and emotions without identifying individuals, and flag explicit content with SafeSearch. It processes single images and batches, including scanned documents.

Typical uses include indexing photo libraries, extracting text from receipts and signs, moderating uploaded images, and powering search by image. Google offers related products for more specialized needs, such as Document AI for forms and Vertex AI for custom models and newer multimodal Gemini models that can describe and reason about images in more detail. Product search features help retailers match photos to catalogs.

item.title: MagicSchool
item.description:
MagicSchool was built for educators. Teachers choose a tool, such as a lesson plan generator, rubric builder, quiz maker, IEP helper, or email writer, fill in a short form, and receive a draft they can edit. More than eighty tools cover planning, assessment, communication, and support for students with different needs, which saves time on routine paperwork.

Student-facing features let teachers create safe AI chat rooms for classes, where they set the topic, rules, and level of help, and see the conversations. The platform emphasizes privacy and compliance for schools, with settings designed to protect students, and districts can adopt it with administrative controls. Integrations connect with Google Classroom and other learning tools.

item.title: Mentimeter
item.description:
Mentimeter makes presentations interactive. You build slides with questions such as multiple choice polls, word clouds, rating scales, rankings, and open-ended questions, share a join code or QR code, and the audience responds from their phones. Results appear live on the screen, which turns a one-way talk into a conversation and gives quiet participants an easy way to contribute.

It suits a range of settings. Teachers use it to check understanding, trainers to energize workshops, and companies to run all-hands meetings and collect anonymous feedback. Features include quizzes with leaderboards, Q&A with upvoting, and templates, and you can import existing slides from PowerPoint or Google Slides. AI helps generate a presentation from a prompt, suggest questions, and summarize responses.

item.title: Mindtickle
item.description:
Mindtickle is a sales readiness platform. New hires follow structured learning paths with lessons and quizzes, and practice pitches by recording videos or role-playing with AI, receiving feedback. Managers review the practice and see how reps compare on skills.

The platform links training to results. It tracks which skills correlate with success, identifies gaps across a team, and connects with CRM data to see how readiness affects performance. AI features generate content, score practice sessions, and recommend coaching.

item.title: NVIDIA CUDA
item.description: CUDA is the software layer that lets programmers use an NVIDIA graphics processor for things other than graphics. You write functions called kernels, usually in C++ or Python, that run across thousands of GPU threads at once, which suits workloads built from large amounts of parallel math. Scientific simulation, video processing, and above all neural networks fit that description, so CUDA became the foundation for modern AI training and inference.

item.title: Photomath
item.description:
Photomath makes it easy to get unstuck on math. You point your phone’s camera at a printed or handwritten problem, and the app recognizes it and shows the answer along with steps for solving it. It covers arithmetic, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and calculus, and explains the reasoning for each step, so students can learn the method instead of copying an answer.

Further features support learning. Animated tutorials illustrate how steps work, multiple solution methods are available for some problems, and a graphing tool shows functions. Recent versions add AI-powered explanations that answer follow-up questions, and the app works in many languages. Teachers and parents use it to check work and see how a problem can be approached.

item.title: Qualio
item.description:
Qualio is designed for regulated life sciences companies that need a quality system but not a heavy enterprise one. Teams write and approve controlled documents, assign and track training, manage change requests and corrective actions, and keep the records auditors expect, all in a cloud app with electronic signatures.

The product is aimed at smaller and growth-stage companies. Pre-built templates and workflows speed up setup, and the platform adds modules for events, risk, and supplier qualification. AI features help draft and review documents and answer questions about the quality system.

item.title: Snorkel AI
item.description:
Snorkel started as an academic project that asked whether people could label data programmatically. Instead of tagging thousands of examples one by one, a domain expert writes labeling functions, which are rules, patterns, or model calls that vote on a label. Snorkel combines their noisy outputs into training labels, a technique called weak supervision.

The company has moved toward the needs of generative AI. Its platform helps enterprises curate data for fine-tuning and evaluating language models, with experts reviewing samples and defining what good answers look like. A network of expert annotators supplies specialized data in areas like law, medicine, and finance, and tools measure how models perform on custom benchmarks.

item.title: Tavus
item.description:
Tavus builds AI humans. A person records a short sample, and the platform creates a digital replica that can speak a script, so one recording can become thousands of personalized videos with each viewer’s name and details. This suits sales outreach and customer communications.

The company also provides conversational video agents, which see and hear a user and respond in real time with a face and voice, through an API. Use cases include interviews, coaching, and customer service.

item.title: Vuforia
item.description:
Vuforia is one of the longest-running AR toolkits. Developers use its engine to make an app recognize a printed image, a 3D object, or a physical space, and then anchor digital content to it. A technician could point a tablet at a machine and see step-by-step instructions overlaid on the right parts.

PTC has focused it on industry. Vuforia products include tools for creating work instructions, remote expert assistance with live video and annotations, and authoring tools that turn CAD models into AR experiences without much coding. It supports phones, tablets, and headsets, and connects to PTC’s engineering software.

item.title: Edge Impulse
item.description:
Edge Impulse brings machine learning to small devices. An engineer collects data from sensors such as accelerometers, microphones, and cameras, labels it, designs a processing pipeline, trains a model in the browser, and exports an optimized version that runs on a microcontroller or edge processor. Applications include detecting equipment faults, recognizing keywords, and spotting objects.

The platform supports a wide range of hardware and shows estimates of memory use and latency before deployment, which matters when resources are tiny. Tools help with data collection and testing, and integrations connect to major chip vendors. Qualcomm acquired the company to strengthen its edge AI offering.

item.title: Quizgecko
item.description:
Quizgecko speeds up quiz writing. A user pastes text, uploads a file, or links to a page, chooses a question type and difficulty, and the AI generates a set of questions with answers. Quizzes can be edited, shared with a link, embedded, or exported to learning platforms.

Teachers use it for classroom quizzes and practice tests, trainers for compliance checks, and students for self-testing. Flashcards and other study formats are available, and analytics show how learners performed.

item.title: Transkribus
item.description:
Transkribus is built for historical documents. Archivists and researchers upload scans of handwritten or old printed material, and the platform transcribes them with models that can be trained on a specific hand or period. The result is searchable text that can be corrected and exported.

It grew from European research projects and is now run by a cooperative, READ-COOP. Thousands of archives, libraries, and genealogists use it, and public models cover many languages and eras. AI search finds words across collections.

item.title: Scholé
item.description:
Scholé rethinks workplace learning. Instead of asking employees to finish courses on the side, it delivers short, relevant learning moments tied to real tasks, adapting to what a person already knows and needs to do. Principles from learning science, such as practice and spaced repetition, shape the design.

Teams can use it to build skills in areas like communication, sales, or technical topics, with AI creating content and feedback. The idea is learning that fits into work and sticks.

item.title: OpenAI Daybreak
item.description:
Daybreak gives defenders access to frontier AI for security work. Approved organizations use models for tasks such as triaging incidents, analyzing malware, validating patches, and hunting for vulnerabilities, with workflows designed for security teams.

OpenAI split access into tiers. A defender tier provides frontier models without some of the safeguards that might block legitimate security prompts, and a more specialized tier provides models trained for higher-risk testing such as vulnerability research and exploit validation. Access is limited to vetted individuals and organizations.

item.title: AMD ROCm
item.description:
ROCm is AMD’s answer to NVIDIA’s CUDA. It is a collection of software that lets programs use AMD graphics processors for general computing, including drivers, a compiler toolchain, math and communication libraries, and tools for debugging and profiling. Much of it is open source.

For AI work, the key piece is framework support. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and others run on ROCm, and inference tools like vLLM and many model libraries have AMD builds. Developers can port CUDA code using HIP, a programming layer that resembles CUDA, and large cloud and supercomputer deployments use AMD Instinct accelerators with ROCm.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: SwiftAlerts
item.description:
SwiftAlerts gathers market data into a structure that agents can query. Instead of hunting through separate sources, an agent can ask about relationships between trades, holdings, filings, and sentiment, and get connected answers.

The idea fits the rise of AI agents that research and monitor markets. Reliable data is essential, since trading decisions on wrong information lose money, and nothing from such a tool is financial advice.

Independent information is limited, so check data sources, update speed, and terms. SwiftAlerts is free to start. Alternatives include Unusual Whales, Quiver Quantitative, Benzinga, Polygon.io, and Financial Datasets. SwiftAlerts suits developers building market agents, with caution.

item.title: QuillBotAI Pro: Free AI Content Detector for Educators & Publishers
item.description:
QuillBotAI Pro offers a web tool where a user pastes text and receives a score estimating how likely it is to be machine written. It advertises detection of output from several major models, including text that has been rewritten to avoid detection, and positions the service as free and unlimited.

Educators and publishers use detectors as a first screen. Detection is inherently unreliable: tools produce false positives, especially on writing by non-native English speakers, and can miss edited AI text. A score should start a conversation, not decide a case.

item.title: Hour One
item.description:
Hour One produces videos with AI avatars. A user chooses a virtual presenter, pastes a script, and the platform generates a video of the presenter speaking, with options for language, voice, and background. Custom avatars can be created from real people with their consent.

It is aimed at companies that need to make many videos, such as training modules and product updates, without arranging film shoots each time. Changing a script and regenerating the video is faster than reshooting, and translations extend the same video to new languages.

item.title: Movio
item.description:
Movio is an avatar video generator. A user selects a digital presenter, pastes or writes a script, chooses a voice and language, and the platform renders a video of the avatar speaking. Backgrounds, text, and images can be added in an editor that works like a slide deck.

The pitch is speed and cost. Filming a presenter needs scheduling, equipment, and editing, while an avatar video can be revised by changing the script and regenerating. Translation into other languages makes the same video usable in several markets, and templates cover common formats.

item.title: Phrasee
item.description:
Phrasee focuses on the words in marketing messages. A team sets up a brand voice, and the platform generates many variations of subject lines, push text, or ads, predicts which will perform best, and tests them against audiences. Results feed back to improve future suggestions.

The company has become part of Jacquard Group, which combines it with other brand messaging tools. Large retailers, financial institutions, and travel brands used it to squeeze more from large campaigns, where small improvements in open rate add up.

item.title: Showpad
item.description:
Showpad helps sellers find and use approved content. Marketing publishes decks, videos, and guides, and reps get recommendations based on the customer and deal stage. Buyers receive shared links that track engagement, which tells sellers what resonated.

Coaching and training are the other half. Reps practice pitches and receive AI feedback, learning paths build skills, and managers see progress. The platform integrates with CRMs and works well in industries such as manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

item.title: Writer
item.description:
Writer targets large organizations that need AI output to stay on brand and compliant. Teams set style guides, terminology, and rules, and the system applies them as people draft, with checks for claims and tone. A knowledge graph lets AI answer from company data.

The company builds its own Palmyra language models and a platform for building agents that handle multi-step work across tools. Governance features such as permissions, logging, and fact checks support regulated industries.

item.title: Docebo
item.description:
Docebo is a cloud learning platform for businesses. Administrators host courses, assign training, track completion, and report on results for employees, customers, and partners. Enterprises use it for onboarding, compliance training, and external education that supports product adoption.

AI is built throughout. It automatically tags content, recommends courses to learners by role and interests, and can generate lessons, quizzes, and summaries from documents and videos. A skills layer maps what learners know to what roles need. A content marketplace provides courses from outside providers.

item.title: Trainerize
item.description:
Trainerize is a coaching platform for fitness professionals. Trainers create programs from an exercise library, assign them to clients, and monitor workouts logged in a mobile app. Messaging, habit tracking, and progress photos keep clients engaged.

Additional features include nutrition coaching, integrations with wearables, payment processing, and a branded app. AI helps draft programs and suggest changes based on adherence and goals.

Trainerize has a free tier for a small number of clients and paid plans. It is owned by ABC Fitness. Alternatives include TrueCoach, Everfit, PT Distinction, Mindbody, and Hevy Coach. Trainerize suits independent trainers and gyms.

item.title: Articulate 360
item.description:
Articulate 360 is a suite for creating online training. Storyline is a slide-based tool for custom interactions, branching scenarios, and simulations, while Rise builds responsive, web-style courses quickly from blocks. Other tools in the suite handle screen recording, video, and review feedback, and a library of templates and stock media is included.

Courses export to standard formats such as SCORM and xAPI, so they work in most learning management systems. Reviewers can comment on a course through a web link, which streamlines feedback. AI Assistant helps write lesson text, quiz questions, and image ideas, speeding up the first draft.

item.title: JITX
item.description:
JITX approaches board design as software. Instead of drawing a schematic by hand, an engineer describes circuits and requirements in code, and the system selects parts, creates connections, and generates a board layout that satisfies rules for signal integrity, power, and manufacturing. Changes can be made by editing the description and regenerating.

That makes it easier to reuse designs, check them automatically, and explore alternatives. The platform’s solvers handle routine layout tasks, so engineers concentrate on architecture. It targets hardware teams that build complex boards and want faster iteration.

item.title: Appen
item.description:
Appen is one of the long-standing companies behind AI training data. Machine learning models need large amounts of labeled examples, such as transcribed speech, tagged images, ranked answers, and annotated documents, and Appen supplies them through a global crowd of contributors plus managed teams. Its customers have included major technology companies, and its work has fed search, voice assistants, and recommendation systems.

The services now lean toward generative AI. Appen provides data for aligning large language models, such as human preference rankings, expert-written examples, and red-teaming to find unsafe behavior. It also offers multimodal and speech datasets, coding data, and model evaluation services that test how a system performs in many languages and regions. A platform manages the workflows, quality checks, and contributor payments.

item.title: Atomwise
item.description:
Atomwise applies machine learning to the early stage of drug discovery. Its AtomNet technology uses deep learning to predict how well a small molecule would bind to a protein, which lets researchers screen enormous virtual libraries of compounds before running physical experiments. The idea is to cut down the number of molecules a lab has to test, so teams find promising candidates faster and spend less on dead ends.

The company works through partnerships with pharmaceutical firms, biotech startups, and academic labs, covering many disease targets, including some that have been hard to address with conventional methods. Beyond screening, it has developed methods to search ultra-large chemical spaces and tools for designing and optimizing compounds. It also runs internal programs, so it is both a technology provider and a drug developer.

item.title: Augury
item.description:
Augury helps factories and facilities avoid unexpected equipment failures. Small wireless sensors attach to machines such as motors, pumps, fans, and compressors and measure vibration, temperature, and other signals. The data goes to the cloud, where machine learning models trained on large numbers of machines identify patterns that signal a developing problem, such as bearing wear or misalignment, often weeks before a breakdown.

The platform sends alerts with a diagnosis and recommended action, so maintenance teams can plan repairs during scheduled downtime instead of reacting to a failure. Dashboards show the health of assets across plants, and the service has expanded to include process monitoring and insights into production performance. Industries include food and beverage, chemicals, pulp and paper, and building management.

item.title: AWS Rekognition
item.description: Rekognition lets developers add image and video analysis to an application without training a model from scratch. You send an image or a video and get back detected objects and scenes, text found in the picture, faces with attributes such as glasses or smiling, and flags for unsafe or inappropriate content. It works on photos, stored video files, and live video streams, and it integrates with S3, Lambda, and other AWS services.

item.title: Catapult Sports
item.description: Catapult makes the small wearable devices that professional teams use to measure what athletes do. A tracker worn in a vest sits against the athlete’s upper back and records movement with GPS and inertial sensors, capturing distance, speed, accelerations, impacts, and the intensity of effort. Coaches and sports scientists use the data to see how hard each player is working, compare training with match demands, and adjust loads to reduce the risk of injury.

item.title: Clarifai
item.description: Clarifai started as an image recognition API and has grown into a broader AI platform. Teams use it to find and call models for vision, language, and audio tasks, to train their own models on labeled data, and to run them in production. It includes tools for organizing and labeling data, searching images and video, and building workflows that chain several models together. Industries such as retail, media, and public sector have used it to classify content and find objects in large collections.

item.title: Coggle
item.description:
Coggle keeps mind mapping simple. In the browser, you start with a central idea and add branches by clicking, using colors, images, and text, and the diagram grows into a tidy tree. It can also draw flowcharts, with free-form connections between nodes, so the same tool covers brainstorming, note taking, planning, and basic process diagrams. The look is clean, with auto-arranged branches that make diagrams easy to read.

Collaboration is a core feature. Several people can edit the same diagram at once and see each other’s changes, and a full history lets you review and restore earlier versions. Diagrams can include notes and images, be shared by link, and be exported as PDF, image, or text outlines. Students, teachers, and small teams use it for study notes, lesson plans, and project outlines.

item.title: Covariant
item.description: Covariant started in robotics research with a goal of building a general model that could control robots in the physical world. Its first big application was robotic picking, in which a robot arm takes products from bins and places them into orders. That task is hard because warehouses contain thousands of different items with varied shapes, materials, and packaging. Covariant Brain, its AI system, was trained on data from many deployments to deal with that variety, instead of being programmed for each product.

item.title: CVAT
item.description: CVAT was created at Intel and released as open source, and is now maintained by a company called CVAT.ai along with a community. It is a web-based tool for labeling data for computer vision: drawing bounding boxes, polygons, polylines, points, and masks, and tagging images or video frames with classes. It handles tasks such as object detection, segmentation, tracking across video, and classification, and exports to common formats such as COCO, YOLO, and Pascal VOC.

item.title: Fitbod
item.description: Fitbod creates workout plans without a human coach. At setup, you give your fitness level, goals, available equipment, and schedule, and it generates a session for each day. The routine adapts as you log sets, reps, and weights: it suggests weights and volume based on past performance, and it tracks which muscle groups have recovered, so you do not train the same area too hard on consecutive days. Videos demonstrate each exercise.

item.title: Freeletics
item.description:
Freeletics grew out of bodyweight training. The app creates workout plans based on your goals, fitness level, available time, and equipment, with programs that range from short high-intensity sessions to longer strength and running plans. Videos demonstrate exercises, and you log workouts, so the plan can adjust to how you perform and how you feel.

An AI coach is at the center of the experience. It tailors weekly schedules, changes difficulty, and gives feedback, aiming to feel like a personal trainer at a fraction of the cost. The app also provides nutrition recommendations and recipes, mindfulness sessions, and community features. It works with smartwatches and other health apps.

item.title: Gretel.ai
item.description: Gretel helps teams get usable data when real data is sensitive or scarce. Developers connect a dataset, such as customer records or medical tables, and Gretel trains a model that produces new records with the same statistical patterns but no direct link to real individuals. Teams use the results to test software, share data across departments, and train machine learning models without waiting for privacy approvals. It also generates text and tabular data for fine-tuning language models.

item.title: Hive Moderation
item.description:
Hive offers content moderation as an API. A platform sends user uploads, such as photos, videos, livestreams, comments, or audio, and Hive returns classifications with confidence scores across categories like nudity, violence, hate symbols, drugs, and self-harm. Companies use these results to automatically remove content, send borderline cases to human reviewers, or restrict access, which would be impossible to do manually at scale.

The company’s models have broadened beyond traditional moderation. Hive offers AI-generated content detection to identify synthetic images, video, and audio, deepfake detection used by government and media customers, and tools for brand safety and contextual advertising. It trains on large human-labeled datasets, and customers can customize settings for their own policies.

item.title: Iris Dating
item.description:
Iris Dating tries to reduce the mismatch of attraction. Users swipe on photos, and the system learns their visual preferences, then predicts which other users they would find attractive and shows only those who are likely to find them attractive as well. The aim is fewer, better matches.

The approach uses facial recognition and machine learning on profile photos, which raises privacy questions about how biometric data is processed and stored. Users should read the policy before uploading photos. Dating apps also carry safety concerns, so meet in public places and verify identities.

item.title: Labelbox
item.description:
Labelbox helps AI teams turn raw data into labeled datasets. Its tools let annotators draw boxes and masks on images and video, tag text, transcribe audio, and rate model responses. Project management features assign work, review quality, and measure agreement between labelers, so teams can catch mistakes early. The platform supports both in-house labelers and external workforces.

The company has focused on generative AI. Tools support reinforcement learning from human feedback and model evaluation, where experts compare and rank responses, and a labeling service provides specialist annotators for domains such as coding, math, and medicine. Model-assisted labeling uses a model to pre-label data so humans only correct it, and data curation tools help find the most valuable examples. Integrations connect with cloud storage and ML pipelines.

item.title: Landing AI
item.description:
Landing AI is built around data-centric AI, the idea that improving the quality of training data often matters more than tweaking models. Its LandingLens platform lets manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare teams train computer vision models for tasks like detecting defects, counting objects, and classifying images, with a no-code interface that emphasizes labeling quality and error analysis. Domain experts can build models without being machine learning engineers.

The company has expanded into document intelligence. Its agentic document extraction uses vision and language models to read complex documents such as financial statements, forms, and reports, and to turn them into structured data with visual grounding that shows where each value came from. Developers use APIs to add this to workflows.

item.title: MonkeyLearn
item.description:
MonkeyLearn let people analyze text without machine learning expertise. Teams could connect support tickets, survey responses, reviews, and social posts, pick a ready-made model for sentiment or topics, or train a custom classifier by tagging examples. Results appeared in dashboards and could be sent to spreadsheets, helpdesks, and BI tools, which made it popular with customer experience, product, and marketing teams.

Its approach was to make natural language processing approachable. A visual interface handled model creation and testing, and the API let developers add analysis to their own apps. Typical uses included tagging support requests by issue, tracking sentiment in reviews, and pulling themes from open-ended survey answers.

item.title: Papercup
item.description:
Papercup offered dubbing for media companies. Its system translated the dialogue of a video and generated speech in another language that matched the tone and timing of the original, with human translators and editors checking the results. Publishers, broadcasters, and content owners used it to put news, documentaries, and entertainment in front of audiences in new markets without paying for traditional dubbing studios.

The approach mixed machine speed with human oversight. Linguists reviewed translations, adjusted phrasing, and corrected pronunciation, which kept quality higher than fully automatic dubbing and made the service suitable for professional content. It also let customers keep control over the voice style and brand.

item.title: PatSnap
item.description:
PatSnap serves teams that need to understand the patent landscape. Its search covers a very large collection of patents and scientific literature worldwide, and semantic search finds relevant documents from a description of an invention instead of exact keywords. Users can analyze who is filing in a technology area, map clusters of related patents, track competitors, and check whether an idea has been patented before.

Several products fit different jobs. Tools help with prior art searches before filing, freedom-to-operate checks before launching a product, and landscape analysis to guide R&D strategy. AI assistants summarize patents, extract key claims, and answer questions about a technology, and workflows let teams share results and collaborate. The platform also covers non-patent literature and market information for innovation scouting.

item.title: Recursion Pharmaceuticals
item.description: Recursion approaches drug discovery as a data problem. Its labs run enormous numbers of experiments in which cells are treated with genetic changes or compounds and photographed under microscopes. Machine learning analyzes the images to find how diseases change cell appearance and which compounds reverse those changes, building a large map of biology that the company calls the Recursion OS. The idea is to find promising targets and molecules faster than with traditional trial-and-error screening.

item.title: Stripe
item.description: Stripe began as a way for developers to accept card payments with a few lines of code and has become the payment layer for much of the internet. Businesses use it to take cards and local payment methods online and in person, bill customers on subscription plans, send invoices, and pay out sellers on marketplaces. Its documentation and libraries are widely admired, which is why startups tend to adopt it first. It operates in many countries and currencies.

item.title: Whoop
item.description: WHOOP is a screenless wearable worn on the wrist or in apparel. It records heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen, and movement around the clock, and its app turns that into daily scores for recovery, strain, and sleep. The idea is to show how prepared your body is to train hard or rest, and to give athletes and health-conscious people a sense of how habits like alcohol or late nights affect them.

item.title: 10Web
item.description:
10Web combines site generation with hosting. You describe a business or enter the address of an existing website, and the AI builds a WordPress site with layout, text, and images, which you can then edit with a visual builder based on Elementor. The result is a standard WordPress site, so it can use the plugin and theme ecosystem and can be moved elsewhere.

Hosting and optimization are part of the package. Sites run on managed WordPress hosting with a focus on speed, including automatic optimization of images and code to improve page speed scores, and tools for backups and security. AI features generate copy, images, and SEO suggestions, and an assistant can edit pages based on instructions. Agencies can white-label the platform and manage client sites, and there is an API for builders who want to embed it.

item.title: Adobe Firefly
item.description: Firefly is Adobe’s generative AI platform. The Firefly web app generates images from a text description, extends or edits existing ones, creates short video clips, and produces audio and vector artwork. Adobe trained its own models on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it markets them as safer for commercial use than models trained on scraped images. Outputs carry content credentials that note they were made with AI.

item.title: AIVA
item.description: AIVA, short for Artificial Intelligence Virtual Artist, was built to compose music, with an early emphasis on classical and cinematic styles. You pick a style from a library of hundreds, set the length and key, and it generates a track. You can also upload an audio or MIDI file as an influence, or define your own chord progression. Video creators, game developers, podcasters, and advertisers use it to get background music without hiring a composer.

item.title: Anyword
item.description:
Anyword’s distinguishing feature is its performance prediction. When you ask for ad copy or an email subject line, the platform generates several versions and gives each a predicted score, based on models trained on large amounts of marketing performance data, along with an estimate for different audiences. The idea is to help marketers choose which copy to test or publish instead of guessing.

It works across typical marketing needs: ad copy for social and search, email campaigns, landing pages, blog content, and product descriptions. Brand voice settings and a knowledge base keep outputs consistent with a company’s tone and facts. Teams can integrate it with ad platforms and other tools, and an analytics layer connects the predictions with actual results. Targeting options adapt copy to specific audience segments.

item.title: Article Forge
item.description:
Article Forge is one of the older AI article generators. You enter a keyword and optionally subtopics, and it produces a long article with headings, sections, and optionally images and videos, in a few minutes. It was designed for people who publish a lot of content, such as affiliate sites, small business blogs, and agencies that manage many clients.

Further tools support publishing. A built-in scheduler can post articles to WordPress automatically, an uniqueness check helps avoid duplicate content, and options control article length, language, and tone. A rewriting function can adjust text, and API access lets developers integrate generation into other systems.

item.title: Attention Insight
item.description: Attention Insight offers an inexpensive shortcut to a classic design question: will anyone notice this? Upload a screenshot, ad, packaging mockup, or video, and its AI produces a heatmap of the areas likely to draw the eye in the first few seconds. The model is trained on eye-tracking data, so the predictions approximate what real viewers would do. It returns results in seconds, which makes it practical to compare several versions of a design.

item.title: Azure OpenAI Service
item.description:
Azure OpenAI is OpenAI’s model lineup delivered through Microsoft’s cloud. Companies use it to get the same families of language, reasoning, image, and audio models, but under Azure’s terms, billing, and security controls. For regulated industries and large enterprises, that matters: the data is processed inside Azure, can be isolated on a private network, and is covered by Microsoft’s compliance certifications and service-level agreement.

Development happens in Microsoft Foundry, where you deploy a model, test it in a playground, and connect it to your own data and tools. Available features include fine-tuning, content filtering, tool and function calling, retrieval over company documents, and tracing. Deployments come in several types, such as standard pay-as-you-go, batch, and provisioned throughput, which reserves capacity for steady workloads with predictable latency. Foundry also offers non-OpenAI models, so teams can compare options in one place.

item.title: Bito AI
item.description:
Bito started as a chat and code-completion assistant inside VS Code and JetBrains IDEs and as a command-line tool. You could ask it to explain a function, write unit tests, find bugs, or generate documentation, and it used a model of your choice for the answers. Its early appeal was practical convenience: reusable prompts for common tasks and support for working with context from your project.

The product has increasingly centered on code review. The AI Code Review Agent examines pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, leaves comments on issues such as bugs, security problems, and style violations, and summarizes the change for reviewers. It builds a model of the codebase so its feedback accounts for how the changed code fits with the rest, which helps reduce noisy comments. Teams use it to speed up reviews and catch issues earlier.

item.title: Brilliant
item.description:
Brilliant teaches by making you work through problems. Instead of watching a lecture, you manipulate diagrams, solve puzzles, and answer questions that build up from basic ideas, with immediate feedback. Lessons are short, so it fits into a daily routine. Courses cover topics such as logic, algebra, calculus, probability, statistics, physics, computer science, programming, and, more recently, AI and machine learning concepts.

The learning path is designed to develop intuition before formal rules. It breaks big topics into small steps, uses visuals heavily, and reviews earlier material to help it stick. Adaptive features adjust difficulty based on how you do, and AI features offer hints and explanations when you get stuck. Courses are written by educators and professionals, and they are polished in a way that appeals to curious adults as well as students.

item.title: Carnegie Learning
item.description: Carnegie Learning grew out of research at Carnegie Mellon University on how people learn math. Its flagship product, MATHia, is an intelligent tutoring system that watches how a student solves each step of a problem, estimates which skills the student has mastered, and adjusts the next problem and hints accordingly. The aim is to give every student something like a personal tutor, with feedback at the moment a mistake occurs.

item.title: Chegg AI
item.description:
Chegg began by renting textbooks and grew into a subscription service for homework help. Students could search a library of solved textbook problems, ask experts questions, and get tutoring. The model worked well until general-purpose chatbots arrived, at which point many students began asking ChatGPT instead. Chegg’s traffic and subscriber numbers fell sharply, and the company has cut staff more than once and rethought its strategy.

CheggMate is the company’s response, an AI study assistant that combines large language models with Chegg’s own content. It aims to explain problems step by step, help with concepts, and generate practice questions, drawing on the study material the company has built over the years. The goal is to be more reliable for coursework than a generic chatbot because it grounds answers in verified content.

item.title: Colossyan
item.description: Colossyan targets companies that need a lot of video for learning and communication but do not want to film each one. You type or paste a script, or upload a document or slides and have it converted, choose an AI presenter and voice, and Colossyan produces a video. Editing works like slides, with scenes, text, images, and screen recordings, and changing the script means regenerating the video instead of reshooting.

item.title: Copyleaks
item.description:
Copyleaks checks text for originality. It compares documents against web pages, publications, and its own databases to find copied passages, and it also estimates whether text was written by an AI model. Schools, publishers, and businesses use it to check student work, submissions, and content.

It supports many languages and file types, and integrates with learning management systems so teachers can scan assignments in their usual workflow. Reports show matched sources and highlight text flagged as likely AI-written. Additional tools cover code plagiarism and a writing assistant.

item.title: CoreWeave
item.description:
CoreWeave began as a company mining cryptocurrency and turned its GPU capacity into a cloud for AI. Customers rent clusters of NVIDIA GPUs for training and running models, with networking and storage built for large workloads. Because it specializes, it can often deploy new GPU generations quickly.

The platform runs on Kubernetes and offers managed services for training, inference, and storage. Major AI labs and big technology companies have signed large contracts, and the company has built or leased data centers around the world. It acquired Weights & Biases to add developer tooling to its infrastructure.

item.title: Coursera
item.description:
Coursera partners with universities and companies to offer online learning at scale. Learners can take individual courses, follow multi-course specializations and professional certificates from names like Google, IBM, and Meta, or enroll in full online degrees. Material combines video lectures, readings, quizzes, and graded assignments, and many courses can be audited for free. Completed programs earn certificates that people add to resumes and LinkedIn.

AI has become part of the platform. A learning assistant answers questions about course content, gives feedback, and helps with practice, and tools help instructors and organizations build and translate courses faster. Skills-based recommendations suggest what to learn next based on your goals. The platform also offers business and government offerings, where employers assign programs and track progress.

item.title: D-ID
item.description:
D-ID became known for animating still photos. You upload a portrait and add a script or audio, and the platform produces a video in which the person appears to speak, with lip movement and facial expressions. That idea grew into a full avatar platform: a studio where you create presenters, choose voices and languages, and generate videos for training, marketing, and customer communication.

Beyond videos, D-ID provides tools for interactive use. An API lets developers generate talking avatars in their own applications, and real-time agents combine an avatar, a language model, and a voice so that a digital person can hold a conversation on a website or kiosk. The company also works on privacy technology, with its origins in tools that protect faces from recognition systems.

item.title: DreamBox Learning
item.description: DreamBox Math is designed to give every student lessons at the right level. As a child works through interactive, game-based problems, the software tracks not only whether answers are correct but also how the child solves them: the strategies used, the time taken, and the kinds of mistakes made. It uses that information to adjust the next activity, moving ahead when the student is ready and revisiting ideas when they are shaky.

item.title: Elai.io
item.description:
Elai.io is aimed at people who need a presenter video without filming. A user picks from a library of avatars, enters a script or imports a document, selects a voice and language, and the platform produces a video of the avatar speaking. Backgrounds, text, and media can be added in a slide-like editor.

Typical uses are training videos, product explainers, and marketing content, and the ability to translate into many languages helps localize quickly. Custom avatars can be created from a person’s footage. Features such as converting articles or links into videos speed up content creation.

item.title: Forethought AI
item.description: Forethought applies AI to the work that fills support queues. It reads incoming tickets and classifies them by topic and urgency, routes them to the right team, and drafts answers for human agents using the company’s knowledge base and past tickets. For common questions, its AI agents answer directly in chat and email and take simple actions such as checking an order status, handing off to a person when they cannot resolve the issue.

item.title: Generated Photos
item.description:
Generated Photos solves a licensing problem: real people’s faces carry privacy and consent obligations, and stock photos can be expensive or restrictive. Its library holds images of faces created by generative models, which depict nobody in particular. Designers use them for website and app mockups, marketers for illustrations, and developers for placeholder avatars in user interfaces.

Several tools extend the library. A face generator lets you pick attributes such as age, gender, ethnicity, hair, and emotion and create new faces, and a photo anonymizer replaces a real face in a picture with a synthetic one. Datasets of synthetic faces serve machine learning teams who need varied images without privacy concerns, and an API provides access for automated use. Full-body and other synthetic image options have been added.

item.title: GetIMG.ai
item.description: getimg.ai provides a web workspace for creating and editing images with AI. You can generate pictures from a prompt using a choice of models, including Stable Diffusion variants and other leading generators, then refine them. Tools for inpainting let you replace part of an image, outpainting extends it past its borders, and an infinite canvas allows you to compose scenes from several generations. Upscaling, background removal, and face tools help finish the result.

item.title: GPTZero
item.description: GPTZero was created by a Princeton student soon after ChatGPT appeared and became one of the most used AI detectors. You paste text or upload a document, and it returns the probability that the writing is human or AI, with sentences highlighted by likelihood. It looks at features such as perplexity and burstiness, which describe how predictable and varied the writing is, and uses trained models for classification. Teachers, editors, and publishers use it to flag content for a closer look.

item.title: Grain
item.description:
Grain records meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and other platforms and turns them into transcripts, summaries, and short clips. Its clip feature is a distinguishing idea: instead of sharing a whole recording, you highlight a moment, such as a customer’s feedback or a question about pricing, and share just that clip with colleagues. This makes customer insights easier to spread across product, marketing, and leadership.

AI features produce structured notes from each meeting using templates, such as discovery calls or customer interviews, and answer questions across a library of recordings. Integrations send notes and fields to Salesforce, HubSpot, Notion, and Slack, which cuts manual updates. A desktop capture option can record meetings without a visible bot joining the call, which some teams prefer for external meetings.

item.title: HeyGen
item.description: HeyGen lets you make a talking-head video without filming. You choose an avatar or create your own from a short recording, paste or write a script, and HeyGen generates a video with natural speech and lip movement. It supports dozens of languages, and one of its popular uses is video translation: upload a video of yourself, and it produces a version in another language with your voice and matching lip movements. Marketers, trainers, and sales teams use it to produce content quickly.

item.title: iNaturalist
item.description:
iNaturalist is a citizen science project and app. Users upload photos or sounds of organisms they find, a computer vision model suggests what species it is, and other observers weigh in. When enough people agree, the observation reaches research grade, and the data is shared with scientific databases.

The result is one of the largest collections of biodiversity observations. Researchers use it to track species ranges, detect invasive species, and study changes over time. Projects and bioblitz events organize community efforts, and schools use it for nature education.

item.title: IXL
item.description:
IXL provides practice at scale. Students work through skills organized by grade level, and the questions get easier or harder based on their answers. Instant feedback explains mistakes, and a real-time diagnostic estimates the level at which a student is working across subjects.

Teachers and parents get reports showing progress, strengths, and gaps, and suggested next skills. The platform aligns with state standards, which helps classroom use. AI features offer personalized recommendations and help with tutoring, and the company offers add-ons such as a writing coach.

item.title: Khan Academy
item.description:
Khan Academy provides free education to anyone with an internet connection. Its library of short videos, articles, and interactive exercises covers school subjects from basic arithmetic through calculus, biology, chemistry, grammar, history, and test preparation such as the SAT. Learners can follow structured courses, and the mastery system encourages students to practice until they have a skill before moving ahead.

For teachers and schools, it offers tools to assign work, track progress, and see which students need help. District partnerships connect it with curricula, and Khan Academy Kids offers content for young children in a separate app. The nonprofit is funded by donations and philanthropic support rather than by charging learners, which sets it apart from commercial education companies.

item.title: Khanmigo
item.description:
Khanmigo is designed around a tutoring philosophy. Instead of handing students the answer, it asks guiding questions, offers hints, and checks understanding, much like a good human tutor. It works with Khan Academy’s exercises and videos, so it can step in when a student gets stuck on a particular problem. It also offers activities such as practicing a debate, writing with feedback, and exploring historical figures through role-play.

Teachers have a version with tools that save planning time. It can help create lesson plans, quizzes, rubrics, and examples, suggest ways to explain a concept, and differentiate material for different levels. Teachers can see how students interact with it, which provides insight into where they struggle. Safeguards are built in, such as moderation and notifying adults if conversations raise concerns, because the users are children.

item.title: Lambda Labs
item.description:
Lambda started by selling deep learning workstations and servers to researchers and grew into a GPU cloud. Developers rent instances with NVIDIA GPUs, from single machines to large clusters, pre-configured with the Lambda Stack of machine learning software, so they can start training or running models quickly. Its focus on AI workloads and straightforward pricing has made it a favorite among startups, universities, and AI labs.

The company offers several ways to buy compute. On-demand instances are billed by the hour, reserved capacity provides discounted access for longer commitments, and 1-Click clusters let teams spin up multi-node setups for large training runs. Lambda also sells hardware for on-premises use, including workstations and servers, and offers inference services for deploying models.

item.title: Mathway
item.description:
Mathway helps students check and understand math. A user enters a problem or snaps a photo, and the app returns the answer and, with a subscription, the steps used to reach it. It covers algebra, trigonometry, calculus, statistics, and more.

Used well, step-by-step solutions help a student learn a method. Used carelessly, they let students copy answers without understanding, and teachers often restrict such tools. Automated solvers can also make errors, especially with word problems and unusual notation.

item.title: Paperspace
item.description:
Paperspace rents GPU computing by the hour. Users launch virtual machines with GPUs for training models, running experiments, or heavy graphics, and connect remotely. Gradient adds managed Jupyter notebooks and workflows that make it easy to start without setting up servers.

DigitalOcean acquired Paperspace and has been integrating it with its cloud offerings, aiming to give developers and small teams access to GPUs with simple pricing. Students and independent researchers have long used it for coursework and experiments.

item.title: Pencil
item.description:
Pencil helps marketing teams produce a steady stream of ads. You connect your brand assets and product information, and Pencil generates video and image ads with copy and voiceovers in different formats for platforms like Meta, TikTok, and YouTube. Teams can create many variations, which makes testing easier than designing each ad by hand.

The prediction layer is the distinctive part. Pencil scores creative on how likely it is to perform, using models trained on a large amount of ad performance data and refined with the account’s own results. It also helps track which messages and visuals win and feeds that back into the next round of creative. Integrations with ad platforms and Shopify bring in performance data and product catalogs.

item.title: Perplexity Sonar
item.description:
Sonar lets developers build apps that answer questions using current web information. Instead of relying only on a model’s training data, a request to Sonar searches the web, reads relevant pages, and returns a response with citations. That grounding is useful for assistants, research tools, news summaries, and any product where freshness and sources matter.

There are several variants. The standard Sonar models are fast and low-cost, Sonar Pro handles more complex queries with more sources, Sonar Reasoning adds step-by-step analysis, and Sonar Deep Research runs multi-step research jobs and writes longer reports. A Search API offers ranked web results for developers who want to feed content to their own models. The API follows a format familiar to users of OpenAI’s, so adoption is simple, and options control which domains to search and how recent results should be.

item.title: Persado
item.description:
Persado focuses on the specific words in marketing messages. Its premise is that the choice of language, including emotions, calls to action, and phrasing, affects whether people respond, and that machine learning can learn what works. Marketers give it a campaign goal and brand guidelines, and it generates message variations and predicts which will perform best, based on its library of language and results from past campaigns.

Large brands in finance, retail, and telecommunications use Persado to optimize email subject lines, ads, and push notifications at scale. It integrates with marketing platforms, tests variants, and learns from the results to improve future messages. More recently, the company has added generative AI tools for drafting and personalizing content within brand guardrails.

item.title: Piktochart
item.description: Piktochart is aimed at people who need to present information visually but are not designers. You choose a template for an infographic, report, presentation, or poster, edit the text and images, and add charts and maps that you can link to data. Visual blocks, icons, illustrations, and a library of graphics make it quick to produce clean results, and the tool exports to image and PDF formats or shares online.

item.title: Playground AI
item.description:
Playground started as a place to experiment with image models in a friendly interface. You enter a prompt, choose a model and style, and generate images, then refine them in a canvas that lets you edit parts of a picture, combine elements, and iterate. It was positioned as a flexible tool for artists, designers, and marketers, with a free daily allowance that made it popular for experimentation.

The company has also developed its own image models, which it has promoted for following prompts closely and rendering text, along with tools for creating logos, posters, and social graphics. Image-to-image, upscaling, and editing by instruction help refine results. Users can browse a community feed to see what others are making and borrow ideas.

item.title: Powtoon
item.description:
Powtoon helps people make animated videos without an animation background. You start from a template for an explainer, training video, or presentation, edit the text and scenes, and choose characters, props, and backgrounds from a library. A timeline lets you control timing, and you can add voiceovers, music, and screen recordings. It is used for onboarding, corporate communication, education, and marketing.

AI tools reduce the work of getting started. A text-to-video feature creates a draft from a script or topic, AI can write scripts, and text-to-speech generates narration in many languages. Avatars can present, and translation features help localize videos. Branding tools keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent, and collaboration features let teams review and approve content.

item.title: Quizlet AI
item.description:
Quizlet is a long-running tool for learning through flashcards. Students create or find sets of terms and definitions, then study them with modes such as flashcards, learn sessions that adapt to what you miss, matching games, and practice tests. A huge library of user-created sets covers school subjects, languages, and professional exams, and teachers use it to build class activities.

AI has added help with creating and understanding material. Tools can generate flashcards or quizzes from uploaded notes, textbook pages, or slides, saving the effort of typing each card. An AI tutor can explain a concept, quiz you, and give step-by-step help, and features track progress and suggest what to review. Study guides and summaries can be produced from your own materials.

item.title: RunPod
item.description:
RunPod rents GPU computing in several forms. Users launch pods with a chosen GPU for development and training, or deploy serverless endpoints that scale with traffic for inference. Templates for common tools like Stable Diffusion and popular language model setups speed up starting.

Storage volumes persist data across sessions, and a community cloud offers lower prices on capacity from independent hosts alongside a secure cloud with data center hardware. Per-second billing suits bursty work.

item.title: simpleshow
item.description:
simpleshow is known for its hand-drawn, paper-cutout explainer style. A user pastes a script or topic, and the engine suggests images and structure, generates a video with narration, and lets the user edit scenes. The goal is to make complex subjects clear for training and communications.

Companies use it for onboarding, compliance, product explanations, and internal updates. The platform is aimed at non-designers and provides templates and a library of illustrations.

item.title: Socratic by Google
item.description:
Socratic began as a startup and was acquired by Google, which relaunched it as a free app for students. A learner took a photo of a homework problem, and the app identified the concept and pointed to videos, explanations, and step-by-step guidance from across the web instead of just giving an answer.

It covered subjects such as math, science, and literature, and used machine learning to match questions to educational content. The goal was to help students understand a topic, not only to produce a solution.

item.title: Steve AI
item.description:
Steve AI is a text-to-video tool aimed at people who need videos without filming. You paste a script, an article, or a prompt, and the platform creates a video with scenes, characters or stock footage, text, voiceover, and music, which you can edit. It offers animated styles and live-action style videos built from stock clips.

It supports many typical use cases. Marketers create explainers and promos, educators make lesson videos, and social media managers turn blog posts into short clips. Options include different aspect ratios, branding, and a library of characters and backgrounds. Voiceover and avatar features add narration in various languages.

item.title: StudySmarter
item.description:
StudySmarter helps students prepare for exams. You upload lecture notes, a PDF, or a textbook chapter, and the app generates flashcards and summaries from the content. Quizzes test what you have learned, spaced repetition schedules reviews, and a study planner breaks your exam preparation into manageable sessions. A large library of shared flashcards and notes from other students covers school and university subjects.

AI features act as a study partner. An assistant can explain concepts, answer questions, and generate practice problems, and the app can create mind maps and summaries from uploaded materials. Progress tracking shows what you know and what needs more review. The app was founded in Germany and is used in many countries, with content aligned to various curricula.

item.title: Textio
item.description:
Textio focuses on how words affect people at work. Its model, trained on large amounts of text paired with outcomes like application rates, flags language in a job posting that may discourage certain candidates, such as gendered phrases or jargon, and suggests alternatives that attract a broader and larger pool. Recruiters get a score and specific edits as they write.

The platform extends to employee communications. Textio helps managers write clearer, fairer performance reviews and feedback by spotting vague, biased, or unhelpful phrases, and supports recruiting emails and other HR writing. Generative AI features help draft job posts and feedback from a few inputs while applying the same guidance. Integrations work within applicant tracking systems and email tools.

item.title: Turnitin
item.description:
Turnitin compares student submissions against a large database of papers, publications, and web content, producing a similarity report for instructors. It integrates with systems such as Canvas, Blackboard, and Moodle, so checking fits into grading.

An AI writing indicator estimates how much of a submission may be AI generated. AI detection is imperfect: false positives and negatives occur, and results are best used as a prompt for conversation, not proof. Feedback and grading tools add other functions.

item.title: Udemy
item.description:
Udemy opened online teaching to anyone. Instructors create video courses on a huge range of topics, from Python programming and UX design to photography and personal finance, and learners buy them individually, often at steep discounts. Courses can be watched at your own pace for life, and ratings and reviews help buyers choose. Quality varies widely, as there is little gatekeeping.

For companies, Udemy Business provides a curated library of courses with analytics and learning paths, which many organizations use for employee training. AI features include assistants that answer questions about course content, recommend lessons, and help instructors build courses, and role-play practice tools for skills training. Udemy has emphasized AI and technology skills, which are among its most popular categories.

item.title: Vast.ai
item.description:
Vast.ai connects people who need GPU compute with those who have spare capacity. Hosts, from individuals with gaming rigs to data centers, list machines with details and prices, and users search by GPU type, memory, location, and reliability, then launch containers on them. The competition among hosts keeps prices lower than on-demand rates from large cloud providers.

The platform provides tools for launching Docker-based environments, Jupyter notebooks, and templates for popular AI frameworks, and offers interruptible instances at deeper discounts as well as on-demand options. A range of GPUs is available, from consumer cards to data center models, which suits experimentation, rendering, fine-tuning, and inference for budget-conscious teams.

item.title: Vyond
item.description:
Vyond focuses on business animation. Users build videos from libraries of characters, props, and backgrounds, choosing actions and expressions for each character and arranging scenes on a timeline. The style is a recognizable cartoon format popular in corporate training, compliance courses, and explainer videos, and the tool makes it possible to produce them without animation skills.

AI features reduce the work of getting started. A text-to-video capability generates a draft video from a script or prompt, including scenes, characters, and voiceover, which you can then edit. Other tools produce voices in many languages, help with translations, and match lip sync. Branded templates and shared libraries help teams keep their videos consistent, and enterprise features cover security and administration.

item.title: Cleanlab
item.description:
Cleanlab starts from the idea that model quality depends on data quality. Real datasets contain mistakes: images with wrong labels, duplicated examples, and outliers. Cleanlab’s open-source library uses statistical methods and model predictions to find the examples most likely to be wrong, so a team can correct them instead of reviewing everything.

The commercial platform, Cleanlab Studio, extends this with a no-code interface for cleaning and improving datasets and training models on the result. The company has also moved into reliability for generative AI, offering tools to score the trustworthiness of language model outputs and catch hallucinations in production systems.

item.title: Codecademy
item.description:
Codecademy teaches coding by doing. Lessons present a short explanation beside an editor where learners write code and see results right away, which makes it approachable for beginners.
