Courses cover languages such as Python, JavaScript, and SQL, as well as web development, data analysis, and machine learning.

Career paths and skill paths structure the learning, with projects and quizzes to check progress. An AI assistant helps learners who are stuck by giving hints and explaining errors, while avoiding simply handing over answers. Business plans let companies train teams, and Skillsoft acquired Codecademy to add it to its corporate learning catalog.

item.title: Diffbot
item.description:
Diffbot uses computer vision and natural language processing to read web pages the way a person would. Instead of writing a scraper for each site, developers send a URL to its APIs and receive structured data about articles, products, or people, regardless of page layout.

The company also built a large knowledge graph, a database of entities such as organizations, people, and products, with relationships collected from across the web. Customers query it to enrich records, monitor news, find companies matching criteria, or give language models grounded facts. Its extraction tools support crawling at scale.

item.title: edX
item.description:
edX was founded by Harvard and MIT as a nonprofit to put university courses online. Learners can audit many courses for free or pay for verified certificates, and the catalog includes professional certificates, bootcamps, and online degree programs from partner universities and companies.

The platform later became part of 2U, a company that builds online programs with universities. edX.org remains a major destination for learners seeking credentials, and offers courses in computer science, data, business, and many other fields. Business offerings train employees. The open-source Open edX software that powers many other learning sites is separate from edX.org.

item.title: PixAI
item.description:
PixAI is built around anime-style generation. Users type prompts, pick models trained for particular looks, and generate images. A feed of community creations offers inspiration, and sharing prompts lets others learn techniques.

Features include image-to-image transformation, model and LoRA libraries, and tools for creating characters consistently. A mobile app and credit system support casual use.

PixAI has a free tier with daily credits and paid plans. Community models can be trained on artwork without artists’ consent, which is controversial, and content rules apply to the platform. Alternatives include Civitai, Leonardo AI, NovelAI, Midjourney with niji, and Tensor.Art. PixAI suits anime fans and illustrators exploring AI art.

item.title: Poolside
item.description:
Poolside focuses on one domain: code. The company trains large models from scratch, using reinforcement learning where the model writes code, runs it, and learns from whether it works. The aim is models that handle real software tasks reliably.

It targets customers with strict security needs, such as defense and large enterprises, and offers deployment in their own environments. Products include a coding assistant and an agent built on its models, and the company has invested heavily in computing infrastructure.

item.title: Ray
item.description:
Ray makes it easier to run Python code across many machines. A developer adds simple decorators to turn functions into distributed tasks, and Ray schedules them across a cluster. On top of this core sit libraries for data processing, training, tuning, and serving models.

It is widely used in machine learning: large model training jobs, batch inference, and reinforcement learning rely on it, and major AI labs and companies build on it. Anyscale, the company founded by its creators, offers a managed platform.

item.title: Vidnoz
item.description:
Vidnoz offers avatar-based video. A user picks from a library of presenters, pastes a script, selects a voice and language, and generates a clip. A template library, a video editor, and tools such as face swap and voice cloning broaden the toolkit.

Marketers use it for explainers and ads, and educators for lessons. A free tier lets users try it, with limits on minutes and watermarks.

Vidnoz has a free plan and paid tiers. Features like face swap and voice cloning carry consent and misuse concerns. Alternatives include Synthesia, HeyGen, Elai.io, D-ID, and Hour One. Vidnoz suits budget-conscious users making avatar videos.

item.title: Amazon Q Developer
item.description: Amazon Q Developer is the successor to CodeWhisperer, and it is built around AWS knowledge. In VS Code, JetBrains, and other IDEs it offers inline code suggestions and a chat panel that explains code, writes tests, and optimizes functions. In the terminal, it adds autocomplete and a chat that can translate plain language into shell commands. In the AWS console and on chat platforms like Slack, it helps troubleshoot services and explains why a resource is misbehaving.

item.title: Averi AI
item.description:
Averi is aimed at early-stage companies with big content goals and small teams. It plans topics, drafts articles, and produces supporting copy such as landing pages and social posts, using information about the company’s product and audience to keep content on message.

The idea is to give a founder something like a content department: a planner who chooses what to write, a writer who drafts, and an editor workflow for review. Output is positioned around ranking in search and being cited in AI answers, which are goals that depend on quality and on the site’s authority.

item.title: FastBots
item.description:
FastBots lets small businesses add a chatbot without developers. A user points the platform at their website, uploads files, or adds frequently asked questions, and it builds a bot that answers customers using that content. The bot is embedded with a snippet of code or connected to channels such as messaging apps.

Additional features include lead capture, handoff to a human, conversation history, and analytics on what visitors ask. Customization options control the look, tone, and behavior of the bot, and integrations send data to other tools. It is positioned as a quick setup for support and sales questions.

item.title: Leonardo AI
item.description:
Leonardo.ai began as a tool for game developers who needed lots of consistent assets. Users generate images from text prompts with a choice of Leonardo’s own models and others, then refine them with inpainting, upscaling, and background removal. Fine-tuned models for characters, environments, items, and concept art made it popular with game artists, illustrators, and designers who care about a particular visual style.

Customization is a major draw. You can train your own models on a set of images to produce consistent characters or brand looks, use reference images to control composition and style, and draw on a canvas to guide generation. The platform has added video generation and animation of stills, along with an API for developers. A community feed lets users see what others are making and borrow prompts.

item.title: NovelAI
item.description: NovelAI started as a tool for writers who wanted an AI collaborator for fiction. In its editor, you write a passage and the AI continues it, with controls for style, memory, and the characters and world in your story. Features such as lorebooks store details about characters and places so the AI keeps them consistent, and you can edit, retry, and steer the output freely. It’s used by hobbyist novelists, roleplayers, and fan fiction writers.

item.title: Obviously AI
item.description:
Obviously AI was built to make machine learning accessible to business users. You upload a CSV or connect a data source, choose the thing you want to predict, such as customer churn, sales, or lead conversion, and the platform tests multiple algorithms, picks the best one, and shows the results in plain language. It highlights which columns most influence the prediction and lets you try what-if scenarios.

Predictions can be exported or sent to other tools, and the platform offers dashboards for sharing insights with teammates. It positions itself for marketing, sales, finance, and operations analysts who have data but no data scientists, and for consultants who need quick models for clients.

item.title: Robin AI
item.description:
Robin AI developed tools for lawyers who spend their days reading contracts. Its platform used language models trained on legal text to review agreements, flag risks, suggest edits to bring them in line with a company’s playbook, and answer questions about clauses. It worked in Microsoft Word and was used by in-house legal teams and law firms for routine commercial agreements such as NDAs, supplier contracts, and sales terms.

The company also combined software with a managed legal services offering, in which lawyers reviewed work and handled volume for clients. That mix aimed to deliver quick, reliable turnaround, with AI doing the first pass and humans checking. It gained attention for fast growth and for partnerships and funding in the legal AI boom.

item.title: Spellbook
item.description:
Spellbook was built to meet lawyers where they work: in Word. As you draft or review a contract, it suggests language, flags missing or risky terms, and proposes edits as tracked changes. You can ask it questions about a clause, have it compare a draft with your standard positions, or generate a first draft from a prompt, always inside the document you are working on.

Features extend to the review and negotiation steps. A library of benchmarks shows how a term compares to market standards, a playbook feature lets firms encode their preferred positions for checking contracts, and agent-style workflows can run multi-step tasks such as reviewing a set of agreements. It’s used by law firms and in-house teams, particularly for transactional work, and builds on leading language models with legal-specific prompts and data.

item.title: Sudowrite
item.description:
Sudowrite is designed for fiction writers. Instead of a generic chatbot, it provides tools shaped around storytelling: a Describe function that expands a moment with sensory detail, Rewrite options that change tone or style, Brainstorm tools for names, plot twists, and settings, and a feature to continue a scene in your voice. Writers can paste their own text and have the AI follow its style.

The platform has bigger story-level tools as well. Story Engine helps build a novel from a premise by generating characters, outlines, and chapters that the writer edits, and it keeps a database of story details so the AI maintains consistency. Sudowrite developed its own model focused on prose, and offers features for feedback and revision. It has appealed to authors who want a collaborator for drafting.

item.title: Synthesis
item.description:
Synthesis grew out of a school experiment. The idea is that children learn best by working together on puzzles, simulations, and strategic games that require reasoning, instead of by memorizing procedures. Sessions are live and collaborative: a small group of children plays through challenges guided by a facilitator, which builds skills in math, logic, teamwork, and communication.

A more recent product, the Synthesis Tutor, uses AI to give each child personalized practice. It adapts to what a child knows, presents math concepts through games and stories, and gives feedback that encourages persistence. Parents get information about progress. The program is designed for elementary and middle school ages and is used by homeschoolers and others looking for enrichment.

item.title: Taplio
item.description:
Taplio focuses on LinkedIn, where personal branding and B2B outreach happen. Users can generate post ideas and drafts in their own voice, find high-performing posts for inspiration, schedule content, and use carousels and templates. The AI learns from successful posts and tries to match your tone, saving time for busy founders, consultants, and sales professionals.

It includes tools beyond writing. Analytics show which posts and topics resonate and how followers grow, an engagement feature suggests relevant posts to comment on, and a lead database helps find and track potential customers. Team plans allow agencies and ghostwriters to manage multiple accounts.

item.title: Thea
item.description:
Thea focuses on learning over answer-getting. A student uploads notes or a textbook section, and Thea creates questions, hints, and explanations that walk through the material step by step, asking the student to think rather than handing over the solution.

Features include quizzes, flashcards, and summaries built from the student’s own materials, which keeps study aligned with the course. The approach aligns with research showing that retrieval practice improves memory.

item.title: Vertech Academy
item.description:
Vertech Academy sells guides and templates for studying with AI. Rather than ad hoc prompting, students follow workflows for tasks such as breaking down a topic, testing themselves, and planning revision, using chat assistants.

The idea is to help learners use AI actively, as a tutor that asks questions, instead of copying answers. Structure may help those who are unsure how to begin.

Independent information is limited, and results depend on student effort. Check what is included before paying. Alternatives include Khanmigo, NotebookLM, Quizlet, and prompts shared freely by educators. Vertech Academy suits students seeking structured approaches to AI study.

item.title: Voicetype AI
item.description:
Voicetype AI lets people speak instead of type. A user holds a hotkey, speaks, and the text appears in the active app, with punctuation and formatting handled automatically. It works across email, documents, chat, and code editors.

AI cleans up filler words and false starts, and supports many languages. Custom dictionaries help with names and jargon. Dictation can speed up writing for people who think out loud.

Voicetype AI has a free tier and paid plans. Independent information is limited, so check privacy and where audio is processed. Alternatives include Wispr Flow, Superwhisper, Dragon, Apple dictation, and Talon. Voicetype AI suits people who want voice typing everywhere.

item.title: Weights & Biases
item.description:
Weights & Biases, often shortened to W&B, grew out of a simple need. Machine learning engineers run many experiments with different settings and want to compare them. By adding a few lines of code to a training script, you log metrics, hyperparameters, system usage, and sample outputs to a dashboard, and see runs side by side with charts and tables. That replaces scattered notebooks and spreadsheets.

The platform has grown beyond tracking. Artifacts version datasets and models so you can trace what produced a result, Sweeps automate hyperparameter searches, Reports let teams share findings, and a model registry supports handoff to deployment. Weave covers LLM apps with tracing and evaluation, and W&B Inference offers hosted model access.

item.title: X-Pilot AI
item.description:
X-Pilot AI is aimed at teaching content. A user uploads a document or slide deck, and the tool builds a video with scenes, narration, and animations. Avatars can present the material, and editors can adjust text and visuals.

It helps trainers who have written material but lack time or skills to produce video. Videos can be translated into other languages.

Independent information is limited. X-Pilot AI has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Synthesia, HeyGen, Colossyan, Elai.io, and Pictory. X-Pilot AI suits course creators turning documents into video.
